posts.quote: Turning 50 and want to look younger? Just tell everyone you’re 60. Check back tomorrow for more life advice.
posts.caption: The bakery lady asked how many candles. I said fifty and she looked like I'd shortchanged her. We settled on sixty. I took home the cake and the extra ten years, and neither has been returned.
posts.first: My neighbor guessed I was fifty-eight last spring. I was forty-nine at the time. I've been holding onto that for six months like a library book I'm not returning. She waves every morning now. I wave back. We've never been closer.

posts.quote: My ancestors could read the stars and know exactly where they were. I walked out of Costco and couldn’t find my car.
posts.caption: I was certain it was row 31. Near the cart return, near the tire center, near a man loading a mattress. I walked it twice. Then I walked row 32 out of spite. A woman in a minivan offered to help if I could describe the car, and I said gray, and she said that's not helping. I found it twenty minutes later behind a pallet of paper towels, exactly where I'd left it, in a spot I have no memory of choosing. The chicken was still warm, which is the only reason I'm telling you this.
posts.first: My sister asked how the trip went and I said fine. She asked why I'd been gone two hours for a chicken. I said it was a long chicken. She hasn't invited me on an errand since, which I've decided is a bonus.

posts.quote: I can still do everything I did at 30. Just not all in one day.
posts.caption: On Saturday I cleaned the garage, mowed the lawn, and walked three miles, and I'd like it noted that I finished before 2pm. By 2:15 I was sitting on top of the washing machine, which is not what it's for, negotiating with my lower back. We reached an agreement. I will not lift anything heavier than a casserole until Wednesday. The dryer buzzed and I let it. At 30 I would have folded those towels and gone out dancing. The towels are still in the dryer. They've been through worse.
posts.first: I tried to explain to my niece that I used to dance until 2am. She asked what time I went to bed on Saturday. I said 8:40. She nodded politely, the way you do when someone tells you they used to be in a band.

posts.quote: I’ve lived through more winters than I can count, and I haven’t liked a single one of them.
posts.caption: Snow started at 6am. By 6:15 I'd found the good boots, the second glove, and a reason to stay in. I stood on the porch for one minute out of respect. It was a short minute.
posts.first: My boots have a hole in the left one that I've been meaning to fix since 2019. Every year the first wet sock reminds me. Every year I buy another pair of wool socks instead. I now own nineteen pairs and one boot problem.

posts.quote: Raise your hand if your dog has stayed right beside you through your hardest nights.
posts.caption: He has never once asked me to explain myself. Walter is eleven, gray in the face, with the posture of a retired bouncer. In March I had a week I won't describe, and every night he walked in, circled twice, and leaned his whole weight against my shins until I sat down. He didn't fix anything. He just made it very hard to leave the couch. I've since learned that was the entire job, and he takes it seriously. He's asleep on my feet right now. Rent is one biscuit.
posts.first: Walter has a rule about the bathroom door. He stands outside it and waits, in case I'm leaving the house through the tub. I've never had the heart to tell him there's only one exit. Last night he sighed at the door anyway.

posts.first: I bought the good tweezers on Friday. Slanted tip, the kind a surgeon would use. I now keep a pair in the car, in my purse, in the junk drawer, and in the coat I wore last winter. I trust none of them to be where I need them.

posts.quote: Funny how the people telling you to calm down are always the ones who wound you up in the first place.
posts.caption: I was perfectly calm until the words 'you need to calm down' entered the kitchen. Last Sunday at 4:30 my brother-in-law stood at my stove and told me to relax while I stirred the gravy he'd asked me to make, for the dinner he'd invited eleven people to, at my house. I was relaxed. I'd been relaxed since 2. I asked him to taste the gravy for me, and he did, and it was hot. I said nothing. He's been quiet since, which I'm choosing to read as calm.
posts.first: For the record, I had set out a bowl of ice water next to the stove. I'm not sure why I did that. It was just there, in case. He didn't ask and I didn't offer. We ate at 5:10.

posts.quote: My back went out on Tuesday. It didn't invite me, and it didn't say where it was going. I'm home with a heating pad.
posts.first: It's been four days. I've decided it went somewhere nice. It sends nothing. No postcards, no updates. I keep the heating pad on out of respect, and so something is still home when it gets back.

posts.quote: You finally get comfortable in your own skin, and then it starts heading south. Thanks a lot, life.
posts.caption: I lifted my arm to wave at a neighbor and my arm kept waving after I stopped. That's new. I had made my peace with the knees, the reading glasses, and a face that does what it wants in photos. I was at ease. I was nearly smug. Then the arm. I looked at it the way you look at a coworker who has quietly been taking credit for your work for years. The neighbor waved again and I said I was just stretching. She said sure. I now wave from the elbow down.
posts.first: My mother told me this would start around fifty-two. I said not to me. She was right to the month, which I haven't forgiven. I called her to say so. She said I know and went back to her crossword.

posts.caption: A leaf landed on the porch at 3:12 and he alerted the whole street. The delivery driver at 3:40 got a sniff and a nap. The system isn't perfect, but it is loud.
posts.first: He barked at the mailman for six years. Last month the mailman brought him a biscuit. Now the mailman is family and the leaves are still the enemy. I don't ask how he decides. It's good to have a ranking system.

posts.quote: Remember when you brought something home, plugged it in, and it just worked? No account, no password, no app, no updates. Dad tossed the manual in the junk drawer, and that TV ran for twenty years.
posts.caption: Our TV had one setting, and the setting was on. Channel 4 came in if you stood by the window. Channel 9 came in if you held the antenna and nobody sneezed. When it went fuzzy someone got up and hit the side, and it worked, which is the repair process I'd like for everything I own. Last week my new TV asked me to sign in, accept terms I didn't read, and update before it would show me anything. Forty minutes. I miss getting up to hit it.
posts.first: My dad kept the manual in the drawer under the phone book, mostly to have somewhere to put it. He never opened it once. I opened mine on Thursday and it just told me to go to a website. I have not gone to the website.
